title: A Queen Tried to Destroy the Entire Royal Family. One Baby Escaped.
paragraphs: A Queen Tried to Destroy the Entire Royal Family. One Baby Escaped.
Athaliah thought she had erased David’s bloodline. Behind a temple door, however, a child was breathing—and behind that child stood a promise God had not forgotten.
There are moments in Scripture that almost sound too brutal to read slowly.
And instead of mourning her son, she reaches for his throne.
Then comes the sentence that should make every parent stop.
“When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal.”
Children carrying the blood of her dead son.
Athaliah was not merely trying to influence the throne of Judah.
She was trying to eliminate every rival who could sit on it.
And somewhere inside the palace was a baby named Joash.
Too young even to know that someone wanted him dead.
And this is where one of the darkest stories in the history of Judah quietly becomes one of Scripture’s most breathtaking pictures of providence.
Because Athaliah almost killed them all.

“But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain.”
There is a phrase buried inside that verse that changes everything:
Not because Athaliah suddenly developed compassion.
Not because her plan collapsed before it began.
A woman named Jehosheba took him.
She removed the child from the slaughter and hid him with his nurse.
The parallel account in 2 Chronicles identifies Jehoshabeath as the wife of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chronicles 22:11).
And then the Bible tells us something astonishing.
Joash remained hidden for six years.
While Athaliah ruled the land, the child she apparently believed was gone was growing up in hiding.
A queen sat publicly on a throne she had seized.
A little boy lived secretly near the house of God.
She could not cancel the purposes of God.
This story is not teaching that believers will always escape suffering. Scripture never promises that. Many faithful servants of God suffered terribly, and many were killed.
Nor does the text tell us that Joash survived because he possessed extraordinary faith as an infant.
The point is more beautiful than a motivational slogan about becoming unstoppable.
God’s purposes are not dependent upon human power.
But she could not make God cease to be faithful.
To understand why this child matters so much, we have to look backward.
Long before Athaliah entered the story, God had made a covenant with David.
“And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.”
The Hebrew word translated “covenant” throughout the Old Testament is בְּרִית (berit).
A covenant is not a casual promise whispered when emotions are high.
God had bound the history of David’s royal house to His redemptive purposes.
That does not mean every descendant of David would be righteous. They certainly were not.
It does mean Athaliah’s attempted destruction of the Davidic royal house sits inside a much larger biblical story.
Because centuries later an angel would speak to a virgin named Mary about Jesus:
“He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David.”
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
Suddenly the frightened baby hidden from Athaliah becomes part of something far larger than palace survival.
And Scripture gives us no permission to turn him into one.
In fact, the later life of Joash gives us a devastating warning against doing exactly that.
But Joash belonged to the Davidic royal line through which God was moving history toward the ultimate Son of David—Jesus Christ.
God was carrying forward a promise.
And perhaps that is why this story reaches into places inside us that history alone cannot touch.
Because some of you know what it feels like to live through a season in which evil appears to be winning.
You watched people lie and prosper.
You watched something precious collapse while God appeared painfully silent.
Maybe the hardest part was not the suffering.
There is no record of thunder announcing his survival every morning.
No daily miracle proving that everything would eventually work out.
Six years while Athaliah appeared to have won.
And sometimes faith is exactly that uncomfortable.
God has not abandoned His throne simply because evil currently occupies the headlines.
God has not ceased working because you cannot see what He is doing.
The Gospel is not “believe hard enough and God will preserve everything you want.”
Christianity does not promise that every marriage will be restored, every illness cured in this life, every career rescued, or every earthly tragedy reversed.
The One whose enemies looked at His dead body and surely thought the story had ended.
That is the heartbeat beneath every Christian hope:
Death does not get the final sentence when Jesus is holding the pen.
But Joash’s story has another twist.
When Joash was seven years old, Jehoiada brought him out.
And Scripture records the eruption of the people:
“And they clapped their hands, and said, God save the king.”
And there stood the child she thought had disappeared from history.
Six years of power shattered by the sight of one living boy.
She tore her clothes and cried:
The woman who had seized the throne now called the restoration of David’s heir treason.
Sin has always possessed an astonishing ability to rename reality.
And rebellion can become so familiar that obedience begins to feel offensive.
Athaliah eventually died, and Joash became king.
It would be tempting to end here.
But the Bible refuses to manufacture fairy tales for us.
And that is precisely why Scripture can be trusted with the uglier parts of our own stories.
Joash began remarkably well under the influence of Jehoiada.
He confronted negligence surrounding its restoration.
He directed resources toward rebuilding the house of God.
“And Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him.”
And something inside Joash was exposed.
Second Chronicles gives the painful continuation.
After Jehoiada’s death, leaders of Judah came to Joash, and the king listened to them. The nation abandoned the house of the LORD and turned toward idolatry.
God sent prophets to call them back.
Then Zechariah—the son of Jehoiada, the very family connected with Joash’s preservation and rise—stood before the people under the Spirit of God and confronted their rebellion.
Joash responded by ordering his death.
“Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son.”
The boy hidden from murder eventually authorized the murder of the man who confronted his sin.
And suddenly we understand something essential.
Joash could preserve David’s royal succession for another generation.
But Joash could not save the human heart.
This is where the story stops being merely about Athaliah and Joash.
Because how many times has God shown us mercy, only for us to wander again?
How many prayers did we pray desperately when we needed rescue, only to become spiritually casual when life became comfortable?
How many times did we say, “God, if You get me through this, I will never forget You”?
We may look at Joash and wonder how someone rescued so dramatically could drift so terribly.
But before judging him too quickly, look at the human heart.
Israel watched the Red Sea open and later worshiped an idol.
Peter witnessed the miracles of Christ and later denied knowing Him.
We know about the empty tomb.
That is why Christianity cannot merely be a religion of trying harder.
We do not simply need better circumstances.
The name “Jesus” comes through the Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous), corresponding to the Hebrew/Aramaic name יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua), related to the idea that the LORD saves.
And Matthew explains His mission plainly:
“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
That is the rescue beneath every other rescue.
Athaliah is frightening because we can see her evil.
Our own sin can be more dangerous because we learn how to hide it.
Sometimes we even quote Scripture while protecting the very thing Scripture is trying to expose.
Jesus did not come merely to make respectable sinners feel religious.
He came calling sinners to repentance and offering forgiveness through Himself.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance—a turning, a change of mind that expresses itself in a changed direction toward God.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
It is not punishing yourself until God feels sorry for you.
It is coming into the light.
It is agreeing with God about your sin.
It is turning from self-rule toward Christ.
And the breathtaking announcement of the Gospel is that the King we rebelled against became the Savior who died for rebels.
Not once we had cleaned everything up.
Not once the shame became presentable.
Not once we had accumulated enough religious achievements.
Not grace that pretends sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters terribly.
Grace means the Son of God bore what sinners could never remove from themselves and offers reconciliation to those who come to Him in repentant faith.
Maybe you opened this because the title sounded like palace intrigue.
But perhaps you stayed because somewhere between Athaliah’s throne and Joash’s hiding place, you recognized something about yourself.
Maybe you have been hiding too.
You know how to appear fine.
You know what people expect you to look like.
But there is a room inside your life you keep locked.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A private pattern you keep promising to stop.
Maybe you have spent years making sure nobody discovers what is behind that door.
And He is still calling you.
The Gospel does not say, “Hide better.”
The Gospel says there is forgiveness in Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from a verb carrying the sense of acknowledging or agreeing.
Stop negotiating with the thing Christ is asking you to surrender.
Stop confusing familiarity with God for fellowship with God.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write your private sin publicly.
Let that simple sentence become your confession that you are tired of pretending and want to walk honestly before Christ.
And when you see someone else write those words, do not judge them.
Because the Church should be one of the safest places on earth for repentant people to stop pretending.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list is currently living through their own six hidden years.
They think God has forgotten them.
They see darkness occupying the throne.
They cannot see what God is doing.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm can advance the kingdom of God.

Even send this to the unbelieving friend who has only ever encountered a caricature of Christianity and needs to see what the Gospel actually says about sin, grace, judgment, forgiveness, and a crucified and risen King.
Because there will probably come a night when Athaliah seems to be winning again.
A night when the headlines are dark.
A night when your prayers feel unanswered.
A night when your own failures whisper that God could never use you again.
The apparent victory of evil is not proof of the defeat of God.
Being rescued yesterday does not make us immune to rebellion tomorrow.
We need the fellowship of believers.
We need correction when pride wants applause.
We need discipleship when feelings become unreliable.
We need brothers and sisters willing to love us enough to tell us the truth.
That is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
And it should never replace giving to your local church or caring for people in genuine need.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching and discipleship resources continue reaching people.
If you want your resources to help glorify God, supporting and sharing Christ-centered work is one meaningful way to participate in spreading the message.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper:
Somebody scrolling tonight may never walk into a church.
They may never open a Bible because someone tells them they should.
But they might stop because they see:
“A Queen Tried to Destroy the Entire Royal Family. One Baby Escaped.”
And somewhere inside that ancient scandal, they might meet the truth about a greater King.
The King Athaliah could never prevent history from reaching.
The King Joash could never become.
The King whose righteousness does not collapse when human applause disappears.
The King who does not merely rescue us from enemies outside us, but saves His people from their sins.
Not good people congratulating themselves for being better than Athaliah.
Not broken people pretending they are already whole.
It is guilty people discovering that the holy God has made a way for sinners to be reconciled to Himself through Jesus Christ.
And maybe your story currently looks nothing like something God would want to use.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be burned.
Maybe there are things you would give anything to undo.
The Gospel does not allow us to rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
Your worst chapter does not become good simply because time passes.
But surrendered to Christ, your failure does not have to remain the final word over your life.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became a herald of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and heard the promise of paradise.
Grace meets truth at the cross.
If the Spirit of God has used Scripture here to expose something, do not merely feel emotional and continue unchanged.
Return to Christian fellowship if you have isolated yourself.
Seek reconciliation where repentance requires it.
Tell your testimony if wisdom permits.
Athaliah believed the story ended with the blood she spilled.
Joash might have appeared to be the answer.
And when that King finally came, humanity put Him on a cross.
For three days, darkness seemed to have written the ending again.
And the pen is still in the hand of the risen King.
What evil calls the end, Jesus can turn into the place where grace begins writing again.
